summary:
Article 347-1 of Cameroon's penal code criminalises same-sex sexual activity between both men and women and carries a maximum sentence of five years' imprisonment. The penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts; an ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1, and the 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Sentences under the earlier provision ran from six months to five years.

Enforcement reaches appearance and gender presentation, not only alleged acts. On 8 February 2021 in Douala, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a following on Facebook and YouTube discussing trans life. Both were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification, and each received five years' imprisonment plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370), the maximum statutory term. They had been held since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before a judge released them pending appeal. Their lawyers, Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu, described the convictions as a political decision reached without proof of any acts. Shakiro later left Cameroon and claimed asylum abroad.

A 2013 appeal shows the same pattern. Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, jailed for five years in November 2011, were acquitted on appeal; the original judge had cited their dress, their speech and their order of Baileys as proof they were gay. Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal. Arrests on grounds of effeminacy or appearance under the colonial-era sodomy law carry sentences of six months to five years.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen that year: since 9 March, security forces had arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity. Gendarmes beat two of them in detention. HRW's senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi said the criminalisation law allows both civilians and security forces to abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

Online conduct is separately criminalised. Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime provides under Article 83(1) for one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or one of those penalties, for same-sex sexual propositions made through electronic communications; Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where intercourse followed.

Earlier prosecutions rest on circumstantial evidence. In May 2005, eleven men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy; the government threatened medical examinations to prove their homosexual activity, they were detained into February 2006, trials were scheduled for March 2006 and they were released in April 2006. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347, among them Jean-Claude Roger Mbede, sentenced to three years at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. On 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car, and in the same month two young men arrested outside a nightclub were convicted on appearance and behaviour alone, the judge holding that speech manner, wearing women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor were sufficient evidence of homosexuality; that verdict was overturned on appeal.

Detention conditions are severe for people accused under these provisions. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as hell. The LGBTQ organisation Alternatives-Cameroon shut down after a police raid, removing a service base, and few lawyers are willing to defend the accused.

Official and media hostility compounds the legal exposure. In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, boosting circulation; the state communication council criticised the privacy invasion, while President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy and prosecutions of people accused of homosexual activity continued. The US State Department's 2010 human rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort, alongside discrimination among societal abuses. A 2020 assessment described Cameroon as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. On 30 June 2024 President Biya's daughter Brenda Biya came out as a lesbian on Instagram, prompting national backlash and, among LGBTQ Cameroonians, hope.
tangentialFactors:
No visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure specific to LGBTQ travellers is documented for Cameroon. The material closest to border practice concerns Cameroonians seeking protection abroad rather than visitors arriving. In July 2010 the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that he is not the only gay person in Cameroon. In August 2011 a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012 the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum-seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding no credible evidence that he was gay, and held him in custody after he threatened to make a fuss on the return flight.

The state's public position that private same-sex conduct is not prosecuted sits against convictions resting on conduct inferred from appearance, dress and messages, and against the 2020 assessment that Cameroon prosecutes consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any other country.

outOfScopeNotes:
No information on legal gender recognition, name change, or identity-document and marker procedures in Cameroon appears in the sources reviewed. No healthcare, HIV or medication access information specific to transgender visitors is documented; the only health-service finding is the 2005 threat of medical examinations to prove homosexual activity among detained men, which is coercive contact with health services rather than care.

No contemporary youth, school or minor-specific legal policy is covered. Historical ethnographic material on same-sex customs among the Bafia people in 1921 has no bearing on the current legal regime and is not treated as visitor-relevant.

No Cameroonian border screening procedure, entry-refusal practice or visa rule for LGBTQ travellers is set out in the sources; the asylum and deportation material concerns outbound cases in the United Kingdom.
